name: Private Market Valuation
title: Private Market Valuation
answer: Private market valuation is the practice of estimating what a company or fund holding is worth when there is no daily public price. It covers venture capital, growth equity, buyouts, private credit, real assets, and fund interests, and it supports deal sourcing, portfolio monitoring, LP reporting, and transaction pricing. In an AI context, it also includes valuing AI-focused startups and assets whose value depends on data, models, compute, and talent. The work sits between finance, accounting, and data analysis, and it often feeds into fairness opinions, fund NAVs, and negotiation ranges.

sections.body: Private market valuation is the practice of estimating what a company or fund holding is worth when there is no daily public price. It covers venture capital, growth equity, buyouts, private credit, real assets, and fund interests, and it supports deal sourcing, portfolio monitoring, LP reporting, and transaction pricing. In an AI context, it also includes valuing AI-focused startups and assets whose value depends on data, models, compute, and talent. The work sits between finance, accounting, and data analysis, and it often feeds into fairness opinions, fund NAVs, and negotiation ranges.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of financial and operational data: audited statements, management accounts, cap tables, term sheets, debt schedules, purchase agreements, and CRM records from deal sourcing. Teams typically store this in data warehouses, spreadsheets, and document management systems, with APIs and ETL jobs moving data between them. Public market comparables can come from daily price feeds, and this site tracks 117 listed AI-related instruments with daily prices that can serve as one input for AI-sector benchmarks. AI tools are used for document parsing, data extraction, anomaly detection, and scenario modeling, but the underlying records still need clean provenance and version control.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts usually triangulate three approaches: market multiples from comparable companies and precedent transactions, discounted cash flow or other income models, and asset or cost-based methods. For early-stage companies, common techniques include backsolving from the last financing round, option pricing models, and probability-weighted scenario analysis. AI and machine learning can speed up comparable selection, extract terms from contracts, cluster similar deals, and run Monte Carlo simulations, but the assumptions still come from human judgment. Deal sourcing feeds this loop by mapping companies, tracking sector themes, and flagging candidates for deeper diligence. This site's 354 merger and acquisition filings can support precedent transaction work when the deal facts are relevant.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights, risk, and provenance matter because private valuations rely on confidential data, management projections, and sometimes material non-public information. Firms typically establish clear rights to use data, strong access controls, audit trails, and documented model versions so an estimate can be reproduced and challenged. Valuation committees, auditors, and limited partners often review the process, and conflicts of interest are usually disclosed and managed. AI adds model risk, data bias, and explainability concerns, especially when outputs influence fund NAVs or deal terms. For AI-related targets, legal and regulatory exposure can affect value, and the site's 148 active AI lawsuits and 219 compliance and regulation pages show the kind of surface that diligence may need to consider.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Private market valuation is moving toward more frequent updates, more data-driven comparables, and tighter integration with deal sourcing and portfolio monitoring. AI is likely to take over more document review, data normalization, and first-pass modeling, while humans keep responsibility for judgment, negotiation, and sign-off. Secondaries, continuation funds, and private credit are increasing the demand for credible interim marks between financing events. Regulators and investors are also asking for better explainability and consistency in how AI-assisted valuations are produced. The direction is not full automation but a faster, more auditable loop between market data, company data, and human review.
